description: "Through which institutional arrangements does urban climate action become possible and durable?"

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_site.py; do not edit. -->

::: {.practical-example}
**A practical example**

Two cities may adopt the same retrofit policy. In one, a public utility finances and manages the work; in another, individual households must organise it themselves. The policy label is the same, but the form of action is not.
:::

<p class="term-first-use">The way authority, money, capability and responsibility are arranged is a <strong>delivery configuration</strong>.</p>

Urban climate policy is often described through its targets, technologies or formal instruments, as though implementation follows once an appropriate intervention has been selected. Yet evidence and ambition do not implement themselves. Climate action becomes operable through particular configurations of authority, finance, organisational capability, infrastructure provision, participation, coordination, sequencing and maintenance.

Modes of Climate Delivery compares how these configurations are assembled across city types, sectors and institutional settings. It asks why nominally similar policies follow different implementation trajectories, how responsibilities and resources shift over time, and which arrangements endure through political, fiscal or organisational change. The purpose is not to identify one preferred delivery model. It is to distinguish recurring mechanisms from context-dependent arrangements, so that apparent policy similarity does not conceal the institutions through which action actually occurs.

::: {.what-this-changes}
**The proposition.** The same intervention can represent a different form of climate action when authority, resources and responsibility are organised differently.
:::

**What this theme does not assume.** A delivery mode is a configuration through which change becomes operable and durable. It is not simply a technology, policy instrument, sector or list of participating actors.

## How this connects

- **Input from [Where New Evidence Matters](/research/where-new-evidence-matters.html):** New evidence matters most when it changes what decision-makers understand about how climate action can be delivered or what it may cause.
- **Next stage — [Consequences for People and Places](/research/consequences-for-people-and-places.html):** Delivery arrangements shape which consequences occur, who experiences them and whether climate action can be maintained over time.
- **Return loop:** Consequences generate new evidence, reveal unresolved questions and revise what other cities may plausibly learn.
